nameStory: This brilliant green bee earned the name 'sweat bee' because it's often attracted to the salt in human perspiration on hot summer days. The 'northeastern' part of its name reflects its range, being most common in the northeastern United States and southeastern Canada.
description: The Northeastern Sweat Bee is a stunning metallic green native bee that looks like a tiny flying emerald. These small but eye-catching pollinators measure about half an inch long and have a brilliant, almost iridescent green sheen that makes them stand out from other bees. Unlike honeybees, they're solitary creatures that nest in the ground and are important pollinators of wildflowers and garden plants. Their vibrant coloration makes them one of the most beautiful bees you'll encounter in New England.

idTips.label: Brilliant metallic green color
idTips.description: The entire body shimmers with an intense metallic green that catches sunlight like polished metal - much brighter and more vivid than any other common bee

idTips.label: Small, compact size
idTips.description: About half the size of a honeybee, with a sturdy, rounded body that feels substantial despite its small stature

idTips.label: Attracted to perspiration
idTips.description: May land gently on sweaty skin, feeling like a light tickle - they're seeking salt and are generally non-aggressive

idTips.label: Fuzzy body texture
idTips.description: Up close, the metallic green body appears covered in fine, branched hairs that give it a velvety texture

idTips.label: Ground-nesting behavior
idTips.description: Often seen entering or exiting small holes in bare soil or sparse grass areas where they create their underground nests

habitat: Look for Northeastern Sweat Bees in sunny, open areas with exposed or lightly vegetated soil where they can dig their ground nests. They're common in gardens, meadows, forest edges, and even urban areas with flower beds and bare patches of earth. These bees prefer well-drained soil and are often found near their favorite flowers like asters, goldenrod, and garden plants.

seasonality.spring: Adults emerge from underground nests in late spring, with females beginning to excavate new burrows in warm soil. Early spring flowers like dandelions and fruit tree blossoms attract the first generation.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when you're most likely to encounter them on flowers or landing on sweaty gardeners. Multiple generations may be active, with constant nest-building and foraging activity.
seasonality.fall: Still active into early fall, visiting late-season flowers like asters and goldenrod before final mating and the last generation preparing overwintering sites.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter underground in their soil burrows, completely inactive and hidden from view until spring warmth triggers emergence.

funFact: These bees are essentially living mood rings - their metallic green color can shift and change intensity based on the angle of light, sometimes appearing blue-green or even coppery, making each sighting feel like discovering a different jewel-toned insect.
confusionNotes: The brilliant metallic green color is so distinctive that it's rarely confused with other bees, though it might be mistaken for a green bottle fly at first glance. Remember: if it's visiting flowers and has a fuzzy body, it's the sweat bee; flies have smooth bodies and different flight patterns.
contextualKnowledge: Despite their name, sweat bees are gentle and rarely sting unless directly handled or trapped against skin. Their attraction to human sweat is purely for the salt content, not aggression, making them one of the most harmless bees you'll encounter.
compareHints: As the only species in its genus found in New England, the Northeastern Sweat Bee is easily distinguished from other sweat bees by its brilliant metallic green color. Other regional sweat bees are typically dark metallic blue, black, or have green and copper mixed coloration, but none match the pure, intense emerald green of this species.
